1005.bp: When someone searches online, the system must decide which documents matter most from billions of options. Most search relies on slow, exact-match methods or huge neural networks that need expensive servers. This paper tackles the middle ground: making 'sparse retrieval' fast enough to run cheaply while still using neural-network-style understanding of what users really mean.
1005.wh: The naive approach—checking every document—is too slow. Smarter systems group documents into blocks and skip whole blocks at once, but figuring out which blocks to skip takes time itself. The real tension is that making skip-decisions faster tends to make your results worse, because you're discarding information about whether documents actually match the query.
1005.ap: The authors propose a simpler way to score whether a block of documents is worth visiting: instead of computing expensive scores for every grouping, they use a lightweight scoring scheme that doesn't waste computation on redundant block-level calculations. They pair this with a compact way to store the index and a configuration that works across different neural retrieval models without retuning.
1005.ww: The insight is that you don't need a perfect score for every block—you just need good enough. By mathematically showing that their simpler scoring preserves what matters for ranking, they prove that you can throw away computation without hurting the actual quality of results. It's like skipping every third decision in a checklist if you can show those decisions don't change the outcome.
1005.po: On real search benchmarks, their method runs fast enough for CPU servers while keeping relevance competitive with fancier approaches. The practical benefit is that dense, expensive models can now run on ordinary hardware at scale, making neural search cheaper to deploy.

1006.bp: To find images, videos, or mixed-media content across different websites, systems need to convert everything into one common form—a kind of universal language where similar things are close together. Most systems use large multimodal models trained to match photos to text, but they're built for generation (writing), not for this comparison task. The question is whether that's the best foundation.
1006.wh: Multimodal models trained to write the next word naturally scatter information across many parts of a neural network. That works for generation, but for retrieval you need everything about an image compressed into one small code. A model trained for writing doesn't learn to do this compression because it's never forced to—it can always write by reading from anywhere. So neural codes from generation-trained models stay diffuse and weak.
1006.ap: The authors restructure the model's internal attention flow and add a new training task: given only the final 'summary' code from the model, try to reconstruct the original image and text. This forces the model to pack all important information into that code. They call this process 'collaborative attention reconstruction.'
1006.ww: When a model has to squeeze everything into one code and then rebuild the input from it, that code must contain everything that matters. The same principle lets you compress a video into a short summary—you lose detail but keep the essence. By training with this reconstruction goal first, the codes become dense and useful, and then regular learning-from-pairs training works better on top.
1006.po: On multimodal benchmarks, images and text matched this way retrieve more accurate results. The practical win is that you can now take models built for writing and efficiently adapt them for the cross-modal search tasks that power image search, video recommendation, and mixed-media platforms.

1007.bp: Recommender systems must decide what to show a user next without experimenting (playing items and watching if they click), because experimenting hurts the current experience. Instead, they learn from logged past behavior. The challenge is that one user might like cooking videos and action movies—two completely different things—and the system must learn to recognize both interests, not average them into mediocrity.
1007.wh: Standard recommendation policies (which just pick the single 'best' item) fail here because they can't represent 'a user likes both X and Y'—they can only output one thing. If you train them with loss functions that reward single peaks, they collapse to averaging position between different interests, producing items nobody actually wants. Even newer diffusion models that generate complex patterns are too slow at serving time when you need an answer in milliseconds.
1007.ap: The system uses a mathematical structure (a 'flow model') that can represent all the things a user might like. First it trains this flow model to mimic the historical behavior patterns. Then it uses a 'value function' (a neural network that learns which actions are good) to identify which parts of that flow represent high-quality recommendations. Finally, it distills that into a single-step policy using an 'advantage condition'—a mathematical switch that tells the model 'pick from the good parts only.'
1007.ww: The flow model works like a map of user preferences, showing all the peaks and valleys. The value function marks which peaks are actually good (users spent time there). By conditioning on high-value regions, you train a fast model to sample only from neighborhoods you know are safe. It's like learning that a user likes both comedies and dramas, then building a fast filter that samples only from those two shelves, not the whole store.
1007.po: Tests on five real datasets plus a live recommendation platform show the method generates recommendations users actually choose, with faster response times than diffusion baselines. The payoff is a recommendation system that serves accurate, diverse suggestions in real time.

1008.bp: Social media spreads misinformation through chains of reposts and comments. Detecting fake news is critical for platform trust. Smart systems look at the structure of these chains (who reposted what) rather than just reading the words, because true news spreads differently than false news. But now LLMs can craft convincing fake posts, making this task much harder.
1008.wh: Graph-based detectors learn patterns from how information spreads: true stories tend to spread in certain shapes, while false stories spread in others. But when an attacker uses an LLM to inject posts that agree or disagree in ways that confuse the detector, they pollute both the text signals and the structural pattern. A detector trained on clean data gets fooled by these adversarial posts because they break the rules it learned.
1008.ap: The authors use a large language model as a teacher, not to detect fake news, but to explain each piece of information: 'This post says X, and it fits/doesn't fit with the overall narrative.' They compute these explanations offline (once, for all data) so no LLM runs at detection time. Then they train the detector to align with these explanations, ignoring posts that contradict the overall narrative and trusting ones that fit it.
1008.ww: An LLM can articulate whether a message contradicts the broader story—and that check is robust because it looks at global sense, not just surface patterns. By using an LLM-written narrative as a stable anchor, the detector learns structural invariances (things that don't change when adversaries tinker). Even if an attacker injects a post that looks structurally normal, if it contradicts the narrative, the detector learns to distrust it.
1008.po: On three real datasets including adversarial LLM attacks, the method catches more fake news than existing methods, and does so without needing to call an LLM during detection (keeping inference cost low). The benefit is a detector that stays robust as generation models improve.

1009.bp: When asking an AI system a question that requires outside knowledge (like 'Who won the World Cup in 2022?'), feeding in many relevant documents usually helps—but reading 10,000 words makes the response slow and sometimes the AI gets confused by contradictions. The tradeoff is real: you want enough context to be accurate but not so much that computation explodes or the model trips over itself.
1009.wh: Current systems trim context by ranking it (most likely to be useful comes first) and cutting off at a fixed threshold. But this assumes all documents are equally important for the task—they're not. One source might be crucial for answering 'when,' while another matters only for 'where.' A fixed cut loses information the model actually needs, and ranking doesn't know what the model will ultimately ask the retrieved facts to explain.
1009.ap: Instead of trimming context before giving it to the language model, the authors teach the model itself to pick what it needs as it's generating the answer. The model is trained with a mechanism that lets it flag which parts of the context window are relevant right now, so it can read selectively rather than scanning everything. This is like a reader skimming for one piece of info while ignoring the rest.
1009.ww: Only the model knows what detail it needs to answer this specific question correctly. By learning to select context as it writes, the model can adapt its reading to the question and the generation so far. When it needs dates, it pulls date-bearing passages; when it needs names, it focuses elsewhere. This dynamic selection is more efficient and more accurate than pre-ranking.
1009.po: Across multiple question-answering benchmarks, answers are more factually correct and latency improves because the model reads less. The practical payoff is question-answering systems that are both faster and more reliable, which unlocks real-time QA for time-sensitive queries.

1010.bp: Recommending products based on images and descriptions is harder than recommending based on past purchases alone, because visual and textual information don't always align—the same item looks different in photos and descriptions. The goal is to build user profiles from mixed signals (what they viewed, what they liked) and item profiles from mixed signals (image, text, past buyers) that actually work together.
1010.wh: When you initialize a user's preference from their viewing history, you get noise: someone who clicked once by accident drags the profile in the wrong direction. For items, you build a graph (item A connects to item B because similar users bought both), but the graph is full of weak links—items that happen to co-occur without being similar. Both noise sources degrade recommendation quality, and they compound when you try to learn from noisy signals.
1010.ap: For users: the system writes out what each user actually did in plain language, then asks an LLM to interpret it ('This user favors outdoor gear and cookbooks'), creating a cleaner profile than raw clicking patterns. For items: instead of relying on raw co-occurrence, the system removes weak graph edges using a statistical threshold, then adds back edges that represent 'if you like this item, you'll like that one' based on which audiences buy both.
1010.ww: LLMs excel at reading behavior and inferring intent—they're trained on human explanations. Using them to interpret history bypasses raw noise from accidents or stale preferences. For item graphs, removing weak edges and strengthening audience-based links creates a denser signal where remaining edges are more meaningful, much like pruning a garden to make it healthier.
1010.po: On multimodal recommendation benchmarks, this approach improves the ability to suggest items users click on. The payoff is that visual and textual features start working in concert, boosting recommendation accuracy for e-commerce and media platforms.

1011.bp: Training a recommender system requires feeding it negative examples—items the user definitely doesn't want—so it learns what not to recommend. Picking those negatives smartly is crucial: bad negatives waste compute and let the model learn wrong patterns. The question is how to automatically identify which items are truly disliked versus items the user just hasn't seen yet (and might like).
1011.wh: Simple strategies (random negatives, picking popular items) create false negatives: they pick items that seem disliked but actually match the user's interests—you just haven't proven it yet. The recommender then learns to avoid items it shouldn't. Hard-negative mining (picking close-but-wrong items) also tends to pick items in the same cluster as items the user did like, which means they might be similar to the target—again, false negatives. You need a way to say 'this item is truly different from what the user likes,' not just 'this item is hard to distinguish.'
1011.ap: The authors model items as points in clusters (unsupervised grouping by similarity). When a user likes an item, they sample negatives from three regions: the same cluster (but with decreasing probability over time to reduce false negatives), nearby clusters (hard negatives), and far-away clusters (easy negatives). They adjust these probabilities as training progresses, like an exploration-exploitation balance in a slot machine.
1011.ww: True negatives (items the user truly dislikes) are structurally different, so they tend to live in different regions. False negatives live near the positive item. By starting conservative and gradually shifting away from the positive cluster, the model learns which nearby items are actually false positives, and trains on true negatives instead. It's like progressively broadening your search circle as you learn more.
1011.po: Across three sequential recommenders and three datasets, this sampling strategy speeds up training and improves ranking quality. The payoff is that recommender systems train faster and learn better from the same compute budget.

1012.bp: Language models can now answer complex questions by using tools (searching the web, running code, checking databases), but orchestrating multiple tools is hard—the model must know when to search versus compute versus check, and in what order. Building agents that reliably use tools well requires large amounts of trajectory data, which is expensive to generate.
1012.wh: If you just prompt a model to use tools, it makes mistakes—calling the wrong tool, missing steps, or looping. Training data of tool-use trajectories is scarce and expensive. Synthetic data from the model itself is biased (it learns its own mistakes). You need data that covers both easy cases (building confidence) and hard cases (learning new strategies), but generating and labeling all of it is labor-intensive.
1012.ap: The system generates synthetic tool-use trajectories in two ways: one that greedily picks steps, and one that explores alternatives. This gives diverse examples. Then it filters out bad trajectories and organizes the remaining ones from simple to hard (curriculum). It trains the model in two stages: first with supervised learning to imitate good trajectories, then with reinforcement learning to refine decisions using rewards for tool coordination and accuracy.
1012.ww: By mixing greedy and exploratory generation, you capture both typical behavior and creative solutions. Organizing by difficulty (easy first) is how humans learn—you don't start with the hardest problem. Supervised learning establishes baseline tool-use patterns, and reinforcement learning refines the boundaries between when to use which tool. A model that starts with supervised imitation learns faster under reinforcement learning than one starting cold.
1012.po: On 13 benchmarks including web navigation, the model chooses tools more effectively and completes tasks more often. The payoff is LLM-based agents that can reason through complex, multi-step problems that require strategic tool use.

1013.bp: When you want to find similar images across two different databases (one from Getty Images, one from Flickr), the visual style differs enough to fool simple matching. A model trained on one dataset often performs worse on another because the appearance, lighting, and composition rules are different. The challenge is matching without any labeled pairs from both datasets to learn from.
1013.wh: Existing unsupervised methods learn from within each dataset (finding groups of similar images) and then try to match across. But internal structure doesn't guarantee cross-domain alignment—a 'group of photos' in one domain might not correspond to a 'group of photos' in the other if the way they're organized is different. Without labeled pairs, the model can easily misalign. You need stable, external guidance that works across domains.
1013.ap: The authors use a pre-trained vision model (one that's seen billions of images) to judge which images are conceptually similar without fine-tuning. They build two concept banks (one per domain) using this external judge, marking image pairs that are confidently similar across domains and confidently different. Then they train with a loss that pulls similar images close and pushes different ones apart, while also keeping images within each domain well-organized.
1013.ww: A pre-trained model has already learned what 'a dog' or 'a car' looks like across styles, so it can provide stable anchors across domains without retraining. By using it to build concept banks first, the model learns from reliable external signals rather than guessing from internal structure. The geometry-based organizing (pull-and-push forces around concepts) maintains structure within each domain while aligning across.
1013.po: On cross-domain image-retrieval benchmarks, this approach finds similar images more accurately than methods that only use internal patterns. The payoff is that search engines can match images across different sources and styles reliably, enabling federated image search.

1014.bp: When evaluating search results, human judges often score multiple dimensions: Is the answer exact? Does it cover all angles? Is it relevant to the question? Using an LLM as an automated judge is cheap but raises a question: can these multi-faceted grades help train the search system itself, not just evaluate it?
1014.wh: Search systems learn to rank by optimizing a loss based on binary judgments (good or bad). Multi-criteria LLM grades are richer but it's unclear how to use them—they look like evaluation signals, not training signals. You could average them, but that loses the information that 'contextual fit' might matter more than 'exactness' for this query. The tension is between the detail in multi-criteria judgments and the simplicity required for training.
1014.ap: The authors treat each criterion grade (exactness, coverage, topicality, contextual fit) as a separate feature in a learning-to-rank model. They train the ranker to optimize based on these features rather than raw retrieval scores alone, using existing evaluation data from human judgments to validate the approach.
1014.ww: Each criterion captures a different reason a result matters. By giving the ranker access to all of them, it can learn that sometimes 'contextual fit' outweighs 'topicality,' depending on the query. It's like telling a search engine 'I know you thought relevance was the main thing, but this question cares more about whether the result is timely.' LLMs grade these dimensions reasonably well, so their output becomes training signal.
1014.po: Results improve by 14-36% in ranking quality, with gains strongest for weaker search systems and complementary for strong ones. The practical payoff is that LLM-based evaluation becomes a training loop: evaluate queries, feed grades back to training, improve system, repeat.

1015.bp: Recommender systems use neural codes (short sequences of numbers) to represent items, then add new items and update these codes as user behavior changes. Updating codes carefully is crucial—change them too much and the model that uses these codes stops working; change them too little and you miss important signals.
1015.wh: New items are assigned codes based on what other users did with them (collaborative signals). But real-world streams add new items constantly and user behavior drifts—what 'similar to other electronics' meant last month might shift this month as new competitors enter. Blindly retraining both the tokenizer and recommender is expensive. Trying to fine-tune just the tokenizer risks flipping codes for old items, breaking the recommender's learned associations.
1015.ap: The system tracks which items are drifting (changing patterns) and which are stable. It fine-tunes the codes for drifting items while keeping stable items fixed. It uses a module that computes 'drift confidence' for each item based on how much its collaborative patterns have shifted. Then it reassigns codes in stages: first loose (allowing more change), then strict (locking in), so the recommender can adapt gradually.
1015.ww: By identifying which items actually changed, you don't waste adaptation budget on items that are stable. The recommender learned alignments between old codes and meanings—codes that didn't change don't break those alignments. Gradual reassignment (loose-to-strict) lets the recommender's weights adjust to the new codes incrementally, like adjusting glasses gradually rather than suddenly changing the prescription.
1015.po: On benchmarks with streaming item arrivals, this approach avoids forgetting old items while incorporating new information. The payoff is a recommender system that adapts to new items and behavior shifts without expensive full retraining or catastrophic breakdowns.

1016.bp: When a researcher or patent examiner reviews hundreds of documents to find relevant ones, they must decide when to stop looking. Look too early and you miss important documents; keep looking too long and you waste time. The question is how to set the stopping point based on the actual cost of missing a document versus the cost of reading more.
1016.wh: Existing approaches try to achieve a fixed recall target (find 95% of relevant documents) without considering why the user needs documents at all. But the value differs: a patent examiner might desperately need every relevant prior art reference, while a researcher doing a systematic review might accept some misses if they've found enough patterns. One person's 'done' is another's 'incomplete.'
1016.ap: The authors use decision theory to derive three stopping rules based on the value of perfect information—a mathematical concept that says: how much would it be worth to magically know if the next unseen document is relevant? If that value is less than the cost of reading it, stop. They weight the rules by the true cost of missing documents versus the cost of reading.
1016.ww: In decision theory, the optimal stopping point is where the expected cost of one more read (reading time plus potential cost of misses) equals the expected benefit (finding a relevant document). By computing this mathematically, the system adapts to different tasks: patent examining (high cost of missing references) stops later; systematic review (lower cost) stops sooner. It respects the actual reason for searching.
1016.po: On patent and medical review datasets, the method recommends stopping earlier (saving effort) when it's safe and continues longer when misses are costly. The payoff is a stopping rule that's tuned to the task, not a one-size-fits-all threshold.

1017.bp: In search engines, users click on results, but clicks don't always mean relevance—a user might click on a result just because it's at the top of the page, even if it's not ideal. Fixing this bias is important for learning accurate ranking. Two-tower models try to separate 'how relevant is this' from 'why did the user click,' but there's a fundamental problem: you can't always tell them apart from clicks alone.
1017.wh: Mathematically, identifiability is the question: given click data, can you uniquely determine what the model's parameters must be, or could many different parameter sets explain the same clicks? If the same documents appear in different positions across many queries, you can separate position bias from relevance. But in real data with sparse positional coverage, this separation breaks down and you can't trust the learned bias.
1017.ap: The authors test whether each parameter is truly identifiable by deliberately changing it, retraining the model on real data, and measuring whether the click-prediction loss increases significantly. If the loss doesn't change when you shift a parameter, that parameter isn't identified by the data—you can set it to anything. If loss increases sharply, it's identified.
1017.ww: Identifiable parameters are constrained by the data: the data is incompatible with wrong values. Unidentifiable parameters are invisible to the data—wrong values fit equally well. By testing this directly on the real dataset and model, you find which parameters the clicks actually inform. This diagnostic works because it doesn't assume infinite data or specific click-logging policies.
1017.po: On simulated and real search datasets, the diagnostic reveals which bias parameters can be learned and which are unidentifiable due to data sparsity or logging policy. The payoff is knowing when a two-tower model has actually learned position bias versus when it's just fitting noise, preventing false confidence in ranking fixes.

1018.bp: Modern neural networks (like ModernBERT) beat older BERT at almost everything—dense retrieval, classification—yet they mysteriously underperform on sparse retrieval, where you're matching keywords in queries to keywords in documents. The mystery deserves solving because sparse retrieval is practical: it works on CPU and is interpretable.
1018.wh: Older BERT uses a limited vocabulary of common words and morphological variations are grouped together. Modern BERT uses a raw, unreduced vocabulary that preserves every spelling variation. This was smart for generation (lossless reconstruction), but for retrieval it means the model wastes capacity distinguishing 'run,' 'runs,' and 'running' when they're the same concept for matching. It's like forcing a keyword searcher to distinguish them instead of treating them as the same.
1018.ap: The authors map modern BERT's vocabulary to a coarser, older-style vocabulary (grouping morphological variations). They preserve the model's learned geometry using a spatial topology method (keeping similar words near each other in the new vocabulary). They also add a calibration mechanism that realigns the model's learned patterns with the new structure without 'dying' neurons or collapsing to dense vectors.
1018.ww: Sparse retrieval benefits from a vocabulary where 'run' and 'runs' are the same token because it reduces the space of possible word patterns the model must learn. Modern neural theory shows this coarse-grained vocabulary reduces the complexity the model must learn, tightening generalization bounds. By preserving the geometry of learned similarity, you keep the model's linguistic knowledge while fixing its vocabulary mismatch.
1018.po: ModernBERT adapted this way reaches state-of-the-art performance on sparse retrieval benchmarks (+4.7 improvement), matching or beating older BERT. The payoff is that you can use modern, more powerful architectures for both dense and sparse retrieval, unifying the field.

1019.bp: In real e-commerce, users interact with items in multiple ways: they view products, favorite items, add them to carts, and purchase. Each interaction type tells you something different. Recommender systems that use multiple behaviors together are more accurate than those using purchase alone. But real-world data arrives as a stream—new views and purchases arrive constantly—and systems must adapt without forgetting.
1019.wh: Most multi-behavior recommendation models are trained offline on static datasets. When data arrives in a stream, retraining them from scratch is expensive. Fine-tuning on new data causes 'catastrophic forgetting': the model unlearns what it knew from old purchases and views. Yet you can't ignore new behaviors, because they carry current user interests. The tension is between efficiency (avoid retraining) and learning (adapt to new signals) while maintaining knowledge (don't forget old patterns).
1019.ap: The system builds a graph of users and items where edges are labeled by behavior type (view, favorite, purchase, cart). It uses incremental graph convolution (updating the graph structure as new edges arrive) and multi-task learning (optimizing for predicting each behavior type simultaneously). It tracks which parameters are changing due to new data and updates them carefully.
1019.ww: Incremental updates let you process new edges without rescan the whole graph. Multi-task learning maintains knowledge across behavior types by forcing the model to stay good at all of them (if it forgets views to focus on purchases, the view-prediction loss climbs). The key insight is that heterogeneous behaviors compete for model capacity—by jointly optimizing, you preserve the balance.
1019.po: On streaming benchmark datasets, this approach adapts to new items and behaviors while maintaining recommendation quality on old items. The payoff is a recommender that stays current as new data arrives without full retraining or catastrophic forgetting.
